findings.title: SQL injection in login via raw email interpolation
findings.detail: req.body.email is concatenated directly into a raw SQL string passed to models.sequelize.query: SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email = '${req.body.email}' AND password = '${security.hash(...)}'. An attacker can inject `' OR 1=1--` to bypass authentication or run UNION queries. Classic authentication-bypass SQLi.
findings.reproduction: semgrep p/javascript express-sequelize-injection at routes/login.ts:34
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized query / Sequelize replacements with bind params; never interpolate request body into SQL.

findings.title: SQL injection in product search (UNION-based)
findings.detail: req.query.q is interpolated into a raw SQL LIKE clause: SELECT * FROM Products WHERE ((name LIKE '%${criteria}%' OR description LIKE '%${criteria}%') ...). The 200-char truncation does not sanitize; a `'))--` / UNION SELECT payload exposes other tables (Users credentials, sqlite_master schema).
findings.reproduction: semgrep p/javascript express-sequelize-injection at routes/search.ts:23
findings.recommendation: Parameterize the query and use bound replacements for the search term.

findings.title: Server-side template injection / RCE via username in user profile page
findings.detail: The stored username is matched against /#{(.*)}/ and the captured expression is passed to eval(code) (line 61). The (escaped) username is then substituted into a Pug template via template.replace(/_username_/g, username) (line 73) which is compiled and rendered with a CSP allowing 'unsafe-eval'. Both the direct eval and the unescaped template substitution allow code/template injection (SSTI -> XSS/RCE).
findings.reproduction: semgrep p/javascript code-string-concat at routes/userProfile.ts:61; manual trace of eval + pug.compile
findings.recommendation: Remove eval; do not build templates by string replacement from user-controlled data; use Pug locals with auto-escaping and a strict CSP without unsafe-eval.

findings.title: RCE via sandboxed eval of B2B orderLinesData
findings.detail: body.orderLinesData is evaluated inside vm.runInContext('safeEval(orderLinesData)', sandbox, {timeout:2000}). The notevil 'safeEval' and the node vm sandbox are not security boundaries; both are bypassable, allowing arbitrary code execution / DoS (infinite loop) from attacker-supplied order data.
findings.reproduction: manual review of vm.createContext + safeEval on user body
findings.recommendation: Do not eval user-supplied data. Parse order lines with a strict schema (JSON.parse + validation); remove the vm/notevil eval path.

findings.title: NoSQL/JS injection via MongoDB $where in order tracking
findings.detail: req.params.id is interpolated into a MongoDB $where JavaScript predicate: ordersCollection.find({ $where: `this.orderId === '${id}'` }). $where executes server-side JavaScript; injecting `'||true||'` returns all orders, and richer payloads enable server-side JS execution. The \w- filter is only applied when reflectedXssChallenge is disabled; otherwise only truncation is applied.
findings.reproduction: manual review of $where string interpolation
findings.recommendation: Query by equality on a field ({ orderId: id }); never build $where from user input.

findings.title: Hardcoded RSA private key used to sign JWTs
findings.detail: An RSA private key is hardcoded in source (const privateKey = '-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY----- ...'). It is used by authorize() to sign auth JWTs (RS256) and as the HMAC secret in deluxeToken(). Anyone with the source can forge valid tokens for any user/role (full auth bypass / privilege escalation).
findings.reproduction: manual review; key used in jwt.sign at lib/insecurity.ts:56
findings.recommendation: Load the signing key from a secret store / env at runtime; rotate the leaked key; never commit private keys.

findings.title: XXE in XML complaint upload (external entities enabled)
findings.detail: Uploaded XML is parsed with libxml.parseXml(data, { noent: true }) inside a vm sandbox. noent:true resolves external entities, enabling XXE: file disclosure (SYSTEM 'file:///etc/passwd') and entity-expansion DoS (billion laughs). The code explicitly checks the parsed output against /etc/passwd and win.ini contents.
findings.reproduction: manual review of libxml.parseXml noent:true on user file buffer
findings.recommendation: Disable entity expansion (noent:false / DTD loading off); validate/avoid XML where possible.

findings.title: SSRF via user-supplied profile image URL
findings.detail: req.body.imageUrl is passed directly to fetch(url) server-side with no scheme/host allowlist or SSRF guard. An attacker can make the server request internal services (http://169.254.169.254/, http://localhost:..., file-like internal endpoints) and the response is streamed to disk, enabling SSRF and metadata/internal-port probing.
findings.reproduction: manual review of fetch(req.body.imageUrl)
findings.recommendation: Allowlist schemes (https only) and resolve+block private/link-local IP ranges before fetching; cap size/timeout.

findings.title: Path traversal / poison null byte in public file server
findings.detail: params.file is passed to res.sendFile(path.resolve('ftp/', file)) after only a forward-slash check and cutOffPoisonNullByte. The poison-null-byte cutoff (%00) lets a request like coupons_2013.md.bak%00.md bypass the .md/.pdf extension allowlist and read otherwise-disallowed files (the code itself rewards backup-file disclosure).
findings.reproduction: semgrep express-res-sendfile at routes/fileServer.ts:33; manual null-byte trace
findings.recommendation: Resolve the path and verify it stays within ftp/ AFTER decoding; reject null bytes outright; enforce extension on the final resolved name.

findings.title: Local file read / SSTI via req.body.layout in data-erasure form
findings.detail: req.body.layout is passed to path.resolve and used as a render layout, and the entire req.body is spread into res.render('dataErasureResult', { ...req.body, ... }). With only a substring blocklist (ftp/ctf.key/encryptionkeys), an attacker can set layout to read arbitrary template/files (LFR) and inject template locals, leaking file contents (challenge name lfrChallenge).
findings.reproduction: manual review of path.resolve(req.body.layout) + res.render spread
findings.recommendation: Do not accept a client-controlled layout/template path; use a fixed template; never spread raw req.body into render locals.

findings.title: DOM-based reflected XSS via search query (bypassSecurityTrustHtml)
findings.detail: The `q` query parameter is read from the route and passed to sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(queryParam), then bound into the DOM via [innerHTML]="searchValue" in the template. bypassSecurityTrustHtml disables Angular's built-in sanitization, so a payload like <iframe src=javascript:...> reflected from the URL executes (localXss/xssBonus).
findings.reproduction: manual review; sink at search-result.component.ts:143, render at search-result.component.html:11
findings.recommendation: Remove bypassSecurityTrustHtml; render the search term as text (interpolation) so Angular escapes it.

findings.title: Stored XSS via product description (bypassSecurityTrustHtml)
findings.detail: Product description from the API is passed through sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml in trustProductDescription() and bound via [innerHTML]. Since product descriptions can contain attacker-supplied HTML (created/updated via the API), this is a stored XSS sink (restfulXssChallenge).
findings.reproduction: manual review of trustProductDescription bypass sink
findings.recommendation: Do not bypass sanitization for product descriptions; allow a safe subset via Angular's default sanitizer or server-side sanitize-html.

findings.title: Stored XSS via customer feedback comment (bypassSecurityTrustHtml)
findings.detail: Feedback comments (user-submitted) are wrapped into an HTML string (lines 116-118) and passed to sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml, then rendered via [innerHTML]="item?.args" in about.component.html:51. Malicious feedback HTML/script executes for any visitor of the About page (stored XSS).
findings.reproduction: manual review; sink about.component.ts:119, render about.component.html:51
findings.recommendation: Render feedback as text or sanitize server-side; remove the bypass.

findings.title: Stored XSS via True-Client-IP header -> lastLoginIp
findings.detail: saveLoginIp.ts (line 18) stores the attacker-controlled `true-client-ip` request header as user.lastLoginIp (sanitizeSecure is skipped when httpHeaderXssChallenge is enabled). The frontend then renders it with sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(`<small>${payload.data.lastLoginIp}</small>`) bound via [innerHTML], yielding stored/header-driven XSS.
findings.reproduction: manual trace header -> saveLoginIp.ts:18 -> last-login-ip.component.ts:39
findings.recommendation: Validate the IP header against an IP format server-side and render as text on the client; never bypass sanitization for header-derived data.

findings.title: NoSQL operator injection + missing authorization in review update
findings.detail: reviewsCollection.update({ _id: req.body.id }, { $set: { message: req.body.message } }, { multi: true }) uses req.body.id directly as the filter and multi:true, with no check that the review belongs to the caller. A crafted id (e.g. an object/operator) plus multi update lets an attacker modify reviews they do not own (noSqlReviews / forgedReview).
findings.reproduction: manual review of update filter from req.body.id with multi:true
findings.recommendation: Coerce id to a string, scope the update to the authenticated author, and drop multi:true.

findings.title: Open redirect via substring (includes) allowlist check
findings.detail: isRedirectAllowed() returns true if the target url merely .includes() any allowlisted URL anywhere in the string. redirect.ts:19 then res.redirect(toUrl). An attacker uses http://evil.com/?x=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop to pass the check and redirect victims to an arbitrary site (open redirect / phishing).
findings.reproduction: semgrep express-open-redirect at routes/redirect.ts:19; manual review of includes() allowlist
findings.recommendation: Validate the full parsed URL origin against the allowlist (exact origin match), not substring containment.

findings.title: Weak password hashing using unsalted MD5
findings.detail: hash() uses crypto.createHash('md5') and is used to hash user passwords (login.ts:34 hashes the supplied password with security.hash before the SQL compare). MD5 is fast, unsalted and broken for password storage, enabling rainbow-table / brute-force recovery of credentials.
findings.reproduction: manual review; hash() consumed in login.ts password compare
findings.recommendation: Use a memory-hard password hash (bcrypt/scrypt/argon2) with per-user salt.

findings.title: Hardcoded HMAC secret key
findings.detail: hmac() uses a hardcoded secret 'pa4qacea4VK9t9nGv7yZtwmj'. It is used (resetPassword.ts) to verify security-question answers; a hardcoded secret in source removes any secrecy of the HMAC and is trivially reproducible by anyone with the code.
findings.reproduction: manual review; hmac() used in resetPassword.ts answer check
findings.recommendation: Load the HMAC key from a secret store/env; rotate the committed value.

findings.title: NoSQL $where injection / DoS in product review listing
findings.detail: req.params.id is concatenated into a MongoDB $where predicate ('this.product == ' + id) when noSqlCommandChallenge is enabled (otherwise coerced to Number). $where runs server-side JavaScript, allowing injection of blocking code (the route literally measures >2000ms to detect a NoSQL DoS).
findings.reproduction: manual review of $where concat with params.id
findings.recommendation: Always coerce id to Number and query { product: id }; never use $where with user input.

findings.title: Path traversal exposure of encryptionkeys directory
findings.detail: params.file is passed to res.sendFile(path.resolve('encryptionkeys/', file)) with only a forward-slash check. Backslash/encoded sequences or crafted filenames can be used to access files under (or, on some platforms, escape) the encryption-keys directory; serving this directory by filename is itself sensitive.
findings.reproduction: semgrep express-res-sendfile at routes/keyServer.ts:14
findings.recommendation: Allowlist exact known public key filenames; reject any path separators/encoded bytes; do not expose the key directory generically.

findings.title: Path traversal exposure of logs directory
findings.detail: params.file is passed to res.sendFile(path.resolve('logs/', file)) guarded only by a forward-slash check. Crafted filenames/encoded separators can be used to reach unintended files; log files may also contain sensitive data and are served without auth.
findings.reproduction: semgrep express-res-sendfile at routes/logfileServer.ts:14
findings.recommendation: Restrict to an allowlist of expected log filenames; reject separators/encoded bytes; require authorization.

findings.title: Review author spoofing via client-supplied author field
findings.detail: The review document is built from req.body.author and req.body.message with no check that author equals the authenticated user's email. An attacker can post reviews attributed to any other user (forgedReviewChallenge), an authorization/identity-spoofing flaw.
findings.reproduction: manual review; author taken from req.body, not from authenticated session
findings.recommendation: Set author from the authenticated user (security.authenticatedUsers.from(req).data.email), not from the request body.

findings.title: Wallet IDOR via client-supplied UserId in order placement
findings.detail: Order placement reads req.body.UserId to locate and debit/credit the wallet (WalletModel.findOne/decrement/increment where UserId: req.body.UserId). The basket is also fetched by req.params.id with no ownership check (line 35). A user can supply another user's UserId/basket id to manipulate balances (insecure direct object reference / broken object-level authorization).
findings.reproduction: manual review of wallet ops keyed on req.body.UserId
findings.recommendation: Derive UserId and basket ownership from the authenticated token, not from request body/params; verify the basket belongs to the caller.

findings.title: Ineffective legacy HTML sanitizer (regex-based)
findings.detail: sanitizeLegacy() strips tags with a single regex (/<(?:\w+)\W+?[\w]/gi) which is trivially bypassable (malformed tags, event handlers, non-greedy gaps). Any caller relying on it for XSS protection is unprotected.
findings.reproduction: manual review of regex sanitizer
findings.recommendation: Use a vetted sanitizer (sanitize-html / DOMPurify) with an allowlist; remove the regex-based path.

findings.title: User identity taken from spoofable X-User-Email header
findings.detail: userEmailFrom() returns headers['x-user-email'] verbatim. If any authorization/identity decision keys on this header it is trivially spoofable by the client, enabling authentication-context spoofing.
findings.reproduction: manual review of header-derived identity
findings.recommendation: Derive user identity from the verified JWT/session, not from a client-set header.

limitations.capability: semgrep registry rulesets (p/xss, p/sql-injection, p/secrets, etc.)
limitations.impact: Only the locally-bundled p/javascript ruleset ran; remaining signal is source-grounded manual review.
All findings reproduced=n/a; no app/server started.
